article.title: What Happens to a Car
article.author: Britta Hedlund
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. They pick up the car after you book, and then it’s just gone for a few days until it turns up at the other end. Most people never think about what actually happens behind the scenes. They probably should because that’s usually where things go right or wrong, and it almost always comes down to steps the customer never sees. Someone Checks the Car Over Before It Even Leaves Before anything gets loaded, a decent operator walks around the car and writes down its condition. Not a glance from three feet away; they’ll conduct an actual inspection. They take photos of every scratch, chip, and dent it already had before it left your driveway. This gets skipped more often than it should. Without it, there’s no way to prove whether damage happened on the road or was already there. Ask to see it before the driver takes your keys. Getting It Onto the Carrier Isn’t as Simple as It Looks For most vehicle transport interstate jobs, loading a car isn't just driving up a ramp and parking. Drivers also worry about weight distribution and how each vehicle’s shape works against everything else already on the trailer. A low sports car and a family SUV don’t go on the same way. If someone gets it wrong, it could mean a scraped bumper or a trailer sitting unevenly. Once it’s in position, it gets strapped down at the points the manufacturer actually built for that job, not wherever’s easiest to reach. Anchor it somewhere else, and you’re putting stress on the suspension over a long trip. The Route Is Almost Never the Direct One Carriers hardly ever take the straight line between two cities. They’re working around weight limits on certain bridges, road conditions, and stops to pick up or drop off other cars heading elsewhere. Your car might be on that truck a lot longer than the map distance suggests. This is where people get confused. A trip that looks like two days on Google Maps can stretch to four or five once you account for real routing and the other vehicles sharing the trailer. They’re Watching the Weather the Whole Time One trip can pass through several different climates: humid coast, dry inland heat, cold mountain roads, sometimes all in the same run. Good operators check forecasts and change plans when things get genuinely risky, especially around flooding or heat extreme enough to affect tyres and components sitting exposed on an open trailer. That’s part of why enclosed transport exists. If a car needs more protection from weather or road debris, it goes in an enclosed carrier instead, for a bit more money. What People Actually Complain About Is Silence Ask around, and it’s rarely damage that upsets people most. An operator who confirms pickup and tells you straight away if something’s running late makes the whole thing far less stressful than one who goes quiet until the delivery call. Some companies offer tracking or a check-in call at key points. It’s worth asking them before you book. Save yourself from the stress of waiting to hear something when others can give you prompt updates regarding the transport. The Last Check Closes the Loop At delivery, the same inspection from pickup happens again. The condition of the car will be checked against the pictures taken from earlier. This is the moment that proves everything actually went fine, which is why the first inspection is really important. Skip it, and there’ll be a lot of misunderstandings and disputes to go through when your car arrives with damages you couldn’t remember.
